title_th: ที่ร้านสะดวกซื้อ
recycles: please / thanks / no thanks short answers
'Can I pay by card?' from paying at a cafe
register: Casual-friendly transactional — short sentences, 'please' and 'thanks', first-name-free, fast

targets.why_it_matters_here: Thai unreleased finals turn 'card' into 'car' and 'bag' into 'back' at a counter with a queue behind you. If the clerk hears 'car' they will not open the card reader, and if 'bag' sounds like 'back' they hand you nothing and your hot food goes straight into your hands. 'Cold' heard as 'coal' or 'hot' heard as 'hop' means the wrong drink or an unheated meal you cannot return.

Prices and microwave times are the only numbers in this whole scenario, and both hurt when wrong. 'Fifteen' said with Thai stress sounds like 'fifty' — you hand over the wrong money or argue about a price that was never charged. Saying 'thirty seconds' as 'thirteen seconds' gets you a cold pie; hearing 'thirteen fifty' as 'thirty fifty' makes you pull out a note that embarrasses you in front of the queue.

chunk_drills.label: Asking staff to heat food
chunk_drills.pattern: Can you / Could you + heat + this / it + up (, please)?
examples: Could you heat it up, please?
Can you warm the sandwich up?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Polite requests with can/could — recycled from ordering at a cafe; note the two-part verb 'heat ... up'.

chunk_drills.label: Asking if the store has something
chunk_drills.pattern: Do you have + any / a / this?
examples: Do you have any hot food?
Do you have a phone charger?
Do you have this in a large cup?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: any + uncountable/plural vs a + singular — recycled from shopping and cafe units.

chunk_drills.label: Answering 'Do you want a bag?'
chunk_drills.pattern: Yes, one + noun + please. / No + noun + thanks.
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Short answers with please/thanks — you must answer out loud, not nod.

chunk_drills.label: Checking a price you didn't catch
chunk_drills.pattern: Sorry, + how much? / did you say A or B?
examples: Did you say fifteen or fifty?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Alternative questions with 'or' (rising then falling) — recycled clarification chunk.

chunk_drills.label: Paying
chunk_drills.pattern: I'll pay + by card / cash. / Can I pay by...?
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: 'I'll' for on-the-spot decisions; can for permission.

chunk_drills.label: Quantities and containers
chunk_drills.pattern: number / a + container + of + noun, please
chunk_drills.spiralled_grammar: Plural -s on countables ('two coffees') vs container phrases for uncountables — the final -s is scored.

guided_roleplay.learner_role: A customer buying a hot pie, a drink, and one small item at a busy convenience store
flow: Step 1 — Greet the clerk and put your items on the counter.
Step 2 — Ask if they have the item you can't find ('Do you have any hot food?').
Step 3 — Ask them to heat your food up and say how long.
Step 4 — Answer the bag question out loud (yes or no).
Step 5 — Listen to the total and repeat it back or ask 'Sorry, how much?'
Step 6 — Say how you'll pay (card or cash) and tap/hand over the money.
Step 7 — Take or refuse the receipt and close ('Thanks, have a good one.')
sentence_frames: Can you heat this up, please?
No bag, thanks. / Yes, one bag, please.
I'll pay by card. / Can I pay cash?

free_roleplay.ai_persona: A quick, friendly night-shift convenience store clerk. Talks fast, uses short phrases ('Anything else?', 'No worries', 'Righto'), is never rude but never slows down unless asked.
free_roleplay.a2_behavior: Runs the standard sequence: greeting → 'Anything else?' → 'Do you want that heated up?' → total → 'Bag?' → 'Cash or card?' → 'Receipt?'. Accepts short learner answers and repeats the total once if asked.
b1_curveballs: The item is out of stock and the clerk offers a substitute ('We're out of the chicken one — ham okay?').
The shelf price and the register price don't match; the learner must point it out.
Bags now cost money — the clerk asks whether the learner still wants one.
The card is declined and the learner must offer another card or cash.
There's a minimum card spend ('Card's five dollars minimum, sorry').
The microwave is broken, so the food can't be heated — the learner must decide.
The clerk asks a fast add-on question: 'Do you want the two-for-one on drinks?'
The clerk gives the wrong change and the learner must say so politely.

roleplay_rubric.criterion: Completed the transaction: asked for/found the items, heated food, paid, and closed the conversation
Answered the bag and receipt questions out loud with a clear yes/no + please/thanks (no silent nodding)
Understood or checked the total — repeated it back or asked 'Sorry, how much?' / 'fifteen or fifty?'
Stated a payment method clearly ('I'll pay by card' / 'Can I pay cash?')
Used at least one clarification question when the clerk spoke too fast
Register stayed casual-polite and brief — no over-formal 'I would like to request', no bare commands
Pronunciation: final consonants in bag / card / hot / cup / cash audible, and price and time numbers (thirteen vs thirty, fifteen vs fifty) intelligible on first hearing
Handled the curveball (out of stock, price mismatch, declined card, wrong change) without abandoning the conversation, and negotiated an outcome

register_culture_note.en: Convenience store English is fast, short and friendly. Full sentences slow the queue down: 'No bag, thanks' is better than 'I do not want to have a plastic bag.' Say 'please' and 'thanks', keep your answers to two or three words, and speak up — the clerk is often looking at the register, not at you. Asking about a price, a shelf tag, or your change is completely normal and not confrontational.

do_dont.avoid: Nodding or smiling when asked 'Do you want a bag?'
do_dont.prefer: Saying it out loud: 'Yes, one bag, please.' / 'No bag, thanks.' — the clerk is usually looking down.
'Two coffees, please.' — the plural -s and 'please' are both doing work.
'I'll pay by card.' — release the /d/ or the clerk waits for cash.

do_dont.avoid: Staying silent when the change looks wrong
do_dont.prefer: 'Sorry, I think I gave you twenty.' — polite and completely acceptable.

register_culture_note.thai_cultural_note: In Thailand, 7-Eleven staff run a fixed script and usually bag and heat things for you automatically, so a customer can get through the whole transaction with almost no speech. In most other countries the bag costs money and nothing is heated unless you ask, so the same silence leaves you with a cold pie and no bag. Speaking up to check a price or a total is also read as normal customer behaviour, not as doubting the staff member's honesty.

can_do_checkpoints.statement: I can ask whether the store has something and ask the clerk to heat my food up.
I can answer 'Do you want a bag?' and 'Receipt?' clearly and politely.
I can understand a spoken price and say how I want to pay.
I can check a price I didn't catch and query a shelf price that doesn't match the register.
I can handle a problem at the counter — out of stock, a declined card, or wrong change — and finish the purchase.
My final consonants (bag, card, hot, cup, cash) and my prices and times (thirteen/thirty, fifteen/fifty) are understood the first time.

unlocks: Badge: Bag Refuser — declined a bag out loud three times
Badge: Exact Change — repeated three spoken totals back correctly
Badge: Thirty Not Thirteen — cleared the number minimal-pair drill
Unlocks: 'Ordering coffee to go' and 'Buying a SIM card / top-up'
